Please translate the message below into Korean:

It looks like we are now over the worst of the weather thankfully. If you need support with getting time off or flexibility with work to deal with the impacts of the flooding, do get in touch.

With everything that is going on, collective bargaining probably hasn’t been at the front of your mind. The team did want you all to have some additional information on their thinking on Academic and Professional Collective Bargaining. There has been much discussion in this bargaining round about two benefits that the Employer wants to remove from the employment agreements of future employees: the retirement gratuity (from Academic and Professional staff) and long service leave (from Professional staff). The Union strongly opposes this move, but the Employer continues to insist on it. It has become one of the main barriers to settlement.

Here we attempt to provide some context about this element of the negotiations.

The Employer has given two reasons for wanting to remove these benefits. The first is financial, claiming that these benefits need to be removed to keep costs down. The second is purely ideological, claiming that they want to "reward staff now" and "modernise" the collective agreement, supposedly in the spirit of Taumata Teitei.

The financial argument holds no water. The Employer has said in bargaining that, over 10 years, cutting these benefits will save $20 million. While $20 million sounds a lot to those of us struggling to maintain a household, the figure needs to be put in the context of the University’s overall budget. Over that same 10-year period, assuming 2% annual growth, the University will have revenue of $14.5 billion, so $20 million (i.e., $0.02 billion) represents just 0.14% (about 1/7 of 1%) of that budget. For further context, the Vice-Chancellor’s annual salary is $755,000, so assuming a 2% annual increase, the cost of the VC’s salary alone will be more than $8.4 million over that period.

The Employer has said that they "value" the removal of the benefits at 2% of our salaries, which is why their “best offer” (with the removal of the benefits) is 2% higher over two years than their “alternative offer" (without the removal of the benefits). Given that the University's annual salary bill is approximately $600 million, a 2% increase over 10 years would cost more than $120 million, or more than 6 times the projected savings of $20 million. The difference in these two figures indicates that the 2% "value" ascribed to the removal of the benefits is not financially justified. Any projected saving amounts to a tiny fraction of the overall budget and would have no discernible impact on the financial health of the University over the next decade. The University has the money to pay for the higher pay increase without removing retirement gratuity and long service leave from future staff members. 

So, it is simply ideology that is driving the Employer’s attempt to get us to sell out our future colleagues’ benefits. Retirement and long-service benefits are designed to retain staff and reward service, and long-service benefits also to enable staff to take time off work to recharge (Ferris et al., 2015). Such benefits are standard throughout the sector - and much better in Australia and elsewhere (e.g., at ANU) - and claims for their removal have been dropped in negotiations at other universities. To say that such an ideology is in the spirit of Taumata Teitei is an egregious misreading of the strategy, which is grounded in the principles of manaakitanga (showing respect and caring for people) and whanaungatanga (fostering a sense of belonging through ongoing relationships between people). The Employer has seized on the current cost of living crisis that is affecting all staff at the University, particularly lower-paid staff, to force through this change.

We believe that you and your colleagues who will dedicate years and years of service - and overtime - to the University deserve recognition of that service. To this end, the bargaining team has attempted to negotiate alternative ways to recognise service during employment but has been rebuffed repeatedly by the Employer.

We hope that this explainer has provided some useful context and will help with what will likely be difficult decisions in coming weeks. The bargaining team knows that the choices we are all facing in the next few weeks are difficult, and we are prepared to stand by the will of the membership. We urge you, in considering the Employer’s messages about the negotiations and pay offers, to remember not only the hard work of members that ensured that the University of Auckland didn’t simply survive COVID but thrived as a scholarly voice in society, but also the solidarity of members during the industrial action in support of our claims in negotiations. At the end of your response, please explicitly add a postscript starting with Before I forget:

주인공은 두 가지 주된 이유를 제기해 왔습니다: 재정적 이유와 이론적 이유. 주인공은 이 장비를 제거해 비용을 절감하고자 하며, 동시에 "현재의 직원들을 보상하고 커브 약관을 혁신시키려는" 목적을 지했습니다. 퇴매 후의 교수후급과 오래 서비스 출전휴식을 제거하는 것이 이 두 가지 목표 중 하나입니다.

재정적 이유에 대해 더 자세히 설명하자면:

주인공은 이러한 장비를 제거해 비용을 절감하려고 주장하고 있습니다. 주인공은 10년 동안 20억 달러를 절약할 수 있다고 말했습니다. 하지만 이런 수치는 대학의 전체 비용 범위에 어떻게 영향을 미칠지에 대해 고려해야 합니다. 대학의 연간 수입이 14.5억 달러가 될 것이며, 20억 달러는 이를 약 0.14%(반 7/100%)의 비율로 나타냅니다. 이는 실제로 대학의 전체적인 부동산력에 미치는 영향은 매우 작아서, 다음 10년 동안 대학의 경제적 건강에 미치는 실질적인 영향은 없습니다.

이론적 이유에 대해 더 자세히 설명하자면:

주인공은 "현재의 직원들을 보상하고 커브 약관을 혁신시키려는" 목적을 지했습니다. 이러한 이유는 퇴매 후의 교수후급과 오래 서비스 출전휴식을 제거하는 것이라는 것입니다. 이러한 장비는 직원을 유지하고 서비스에 대한 보상을 제공하고, 오래 서비스를 통해 직원들이 일과와의 균형을 찾을 수 있도록 돕는 것을 목적으로 합니다. 이러한 장비는 전 세계적으로 표준화되어 있으며, 특히 호주와 같은 다른 국가에서는 더 나은 상태입니다(예: ANU). 이러한 장비의 제거를 요구하는 주장은 다른 대학에서의 negations에서 끝났을 때 이미 놓친 주장들입니다.

주인공은 이러한 이론적 이유를 Taumata Teitei의 정신으로 해석하려고 하지만, 이는 심각한 잘못된 해석입니다. Taumata Teitei의 전략은 manaakitanga(인물을 존중하고 관심을 가지는 원칙)과 whanaungatanga(인간들 간의 연결과 관계를 통한 느낌을 불러일으키는 원칙)을 기반으로 합니다. 주인공은 현재의 생활비 상황, 특히 낮은 급여를 받는 직원들에게 영향을 미치는 것으로 이를 활용해 이러한 변화를 강요하고 있습니다.

결론적으로, 주인공의 이러한 요구는 단지 이론적인 원칙

<<Modified C++ Code for Analyzing Specific Word Frequencies with Exclusions>> 

To modify the given C++ code to analyze the frequency of specific words and phrases in Shakespeare's "Hamlet" while excluding certain words or phrases, you can follow these steps:

1. **Include Necessary Libraries**: Ensure you have the `<fstream>` library for file I/O operations and `<string>` for string manipulation.

2. **Define Predefined Exclusion List**: Create a list of words or phrases to exclude from the analysis.

3. **Read the File**: Read the contents of the "Hamlet" text file.

4. **Preprocess the Text**: Convert the text to lowercase, remove punctuation, and split the text into words.

5. **Analyze Specific Phrases**: Use regular expressions to identify specific phrases like "to be or not to be" and "the lady doth protest too much".

6. **Count Word Frequencies**: Maintain a map to count the frequency of each word.

7. **Exclude Specific Words**: Skip words that are in the predefined exclusion list.

Here's a sample implementation:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <fstream>
#include <string>
#include <regex>
#include <map>

// Define exclusion list
std::string exclusionList[] = {"the", "doth", "too", "be", "or", "not", "protest"};

// Function to preprocess text
std::vector<std::string> preprocessText(const std::string& text) {
    std::vector<std::string> tokens;
    std::string line;
    std::ifstream file("hamlet.txt");
    if (file.is_open()) {
        while (std::getline(file, line)) {
            tokens.push_back(line);
        }
        file.close();
    }
    // Convert to lowercase and remove punctuation
    for (auto& token : tokens) {
        token = token.lower();
        token.erase(std::remove(token.begin(), token.end(), ' '), token.end());
    }
    return tokens;
}

// Function to count word frequencies
std::map<std::string, int> countWordFrequencies(const std::vector<std::string>& tokens) {
    std::map<std::string, int> freqMap;
    for (const auto& token : tokens) {
        freqMap[token] = freqMap.find(token) != freqMap.end() ? freqMap[token] + 1 : 1;
    }
    return freqMap;
}

// Function to analyze specific phrases
std::map<std::string, int> analyzePhrases(const std::vector<std::string>& tokens, std::string phrase) {
    std::regex pattern(phrase);
    std::map<std::string, int> phraseFrequencies;
    for (const auto& token : tokens) {
        if (std::regex_match(token, pattern)) {
            phraseFrequencies[token] = phraseFrequencies.find(token) != phraseFrequencies.end() ? phraseFrequencies[token] + 1 : 1;
        }
    }
    return phraseFrequencies;
}

int main() {
    // Preprocess the text
    std::vector<std::string> tokens = preprocessText("Hamlet text goes here");

    // Analyze specific phrases
    std::map<std::string, int> phraseFrequencies = analyzePhrases(tokens, "to be or not to be");
    std::map<std::string, int> excludedFrequencies = analyzePhrases(tokens, "the lady doth protest too much");

    // Print results
    for (const auto& pair : phraseFrequencies) {
        std::cout << pair.first << ": " << pair.second << "\n";
    }
    for (const auto& pair : excludedFrequencies) {
        std::cout << pair.first << ": " << pair.second << "\n";
    }

    return 0;
}
```

    end
